Passage 1: The Four-Point Verification Meeting

A
At the end of each academic year, the staff at Northbridge Adult Education Centre hold a “Week 52 Review” to check four key areas: teaching quality, student progress, resource management, and staff development. This year, the meeting took place on a rainy Friday afternoon in the centre’s main hall. The principal, Ms. Chen, opened the meeting by reminding everyone that the purpose was not to assign blame but to identify what had worked and what needed improvement. She emphasised that the review would lead to a short, practical checklist for the following year, not a long report that nobody would read. The centre, which serves around 1,200 adult learners, has run this review for the past six years, and each year the format has been refined to make it more focused and less bureaucratic. This year, for the first time, the meeting was streamed online so that part-time staff who could not attend in person could still contribute. About 15 staff members joined remotely, and their comments were collected via a shared document.

B
The first point on the agenda was teaching quality. The centre had introduced a new peer observation scheme in September, where teachers visited each other’s classes and gave feedback. According to the coordinator, Mr. Patel, 18 out of 22 teachers had completed at least two observations by May. The feedback was generally positive, but several teachers noted that the observation form was too long and focused too much on paperwork. One teacher, Ms. Wong, suggested simplifying the form to three core questions: Was the lesson goal clear? Were students engaged? What could be improved? The group agreed to pilot this shorter form in the autumn term. In addition, the team discussed the possibility of recording some lessons for self-reflection, but concerns about privacy and consent meant that this idea was postponed for further discussion. Mr. Patel also reported that the number of teachers volunteering to be observed had increased compared to the previous year, which he saw as a sign of growing trust in the process.

C
The second point was student progress. The centre uses a range of assessments, including end-of-term tests and portfolio work. Data showed that 76% of students achieved their target grade in the final exam, up from 68% the previous year. However, the progress of students in evening classes was lower, with only 65% meeting their target. The discussion revealed that evening students often missed classes due to work commitments and had less access to the online resources because the library closed at 6 p.m. The team decided to extend online resource access to 24 hours and to offer recorded sessions for evening classes. They also considered introducing a buddy system where evening students could pair up for study support, but this was left for the student council to explore. The progress data also showed that students who attended at least 80% of classes were significantly more likely to achieve their target, reinforcing the importance of attendance.

D
The third point, resource management, covered budgets, equipment, and classroom space. The centre had spent 92% of its annual budget by the end of May, which was within the planned limit. However, the purchase of new tablets for the language lab had been delayed due to supplier issues. The IT manager, Mr. Li, reported that the tablets would arrive in July, in time for the new academic year. The team also discussed the shortage of quiet study rooms. They agreed to convert a storage room into a small study area with six desks, which would be available from September. In addition, the centre planned to install a water fountain in the corridor to reduce plastic waste, a suggestion that came from the student feedback survey. The budget for these small improvements would come from the contingency fund, which had not been used this year.

E
The final point was staff development. The centre had run six workshops during the year, covering topics such as classroom management, digital tools, and supporting students with dyslexia. Attendance was mandatory, but feedback showed that the workshops on digital tools were the most popular, while the dyslexia workshop was considered too theoretical. The staff development officer, Dr. Ahmed, proposed that next year’s workshops should include more practical case studies and follow-up sessions. She also suggested creating a peer mentoring system where experienced teachers could support new staff. The principal noted that the centre had recently hired five new teachers, and that mentoring would be particularly valuable for them. Dr. Ahmed agreed to draft a mentoring plan by the end of the summer.

F
After the four points were discussed, the principal summarised the decisions. She asked the coordinators to draft a one-page checklist by the end of June, covering the key actions: simplify the observation form, extend online access, convert the storage room, and revise the workshop format. She stressed that the checklist should be reviewed in October to see if the actions were having an effect. The meeting ended with a vote of thanks to the staff for their hard work during the year. Ms. Chen also announced that the centre had received a small grant from the local council to support digital innovation, which would be used to purchase additional software for the language lab.

Passage 2: Designing a Pre-Exam Checklist: Principles and Pitfalls

A
As the academic year draws to a close, many teachers and students turn to checklists to prepare for exams. A checklist is a simple list of items to be checked or actions to be taken. However, not all checklists are equally effective. Research in cognitive psychology suggests that checklists work best when they are short, specific, and focused on key errors rather than covering every possible detail. A checklist that is too long can overwhelm users and may be ignored altogether. In educational settings, checklists are used for various purposes: to guide revision, to ensure that exam instructions are followed, and to help students monitor their own progress. Yet the same principles apply across these different uses.

B
One of the main principles of effective checklist design is to prioritise. In the context of exam preparation, this means identifying the most common mistakes that students make and addressing those first. For example, if a class frequently forgets to use the correct tense in writing tasks, the checklist should include a reminder to check verb forms. Similarly, if students often misread instructions, the checklist should prompt them to underline key words in the question. By focusing on frequent errors, the checklist becomes a practical tool rather than a generic list. Teachers can gather this information from past exam scripts, from classroom observations, or simply by asking students which parts they find most difficult. The key is to base the checklist on evidence rather than guesswork.

C
Another principle is to make the checklist actionable. Each item should describe a specific action that the user can take, rather than a vague goal. For instance, instead of writing “improve grammar,” a checklist item might say “check subject-verb agreement in the first paragraph.” Actionable items are easier to follow and allow users to tick them off as they complete them, which provides a sense of progress. This sense of progress can be motivating, especially for students who feel anxious about exams. Moreover, actionable items make it easier for teachers to give feedback: they can refer directly to a checklist item when discussing a student’s work.

D
However, there are pitfalls to avoid. One common mistake is to create a checklist that is too general. A list that says “review all topics” is not helpful because it does not guide the user on what to do specifically. Another pitfall is to make the checklist too rigid. Exams can vary in format and content, so a checklist should allow some flexibility. For example, a checklist for a writing exam might include a step to “check the word count,” but the exact word limit may differ between tasks, so the user needs to adapt the checklist to the specific exam. A third pitfall is to treat the checklist as a one-off document. Checklists that are created and then forgotten are unlikely to have any lasting impact.

E
A further consideration is the timing of checklist use. Checklists are most effective when used regularly during the revision period, not just on the day before the exam. Teachers can incorporate checklist reviews into weekly lessons, asking students to reflect on which items they have mastered and which need more practice. This regular use helps to embed good habits and reduces last-minute panic. Some teachers also encourage students to keep a checklist journal, where they note which items they have used and how useful they found them. This reflective practice can deepen students’ awareness of their own learning strategies.

F
Finally, checklists should be reviewed and updated. What works for one group of students may not work for another. After an exam, teachers and students can evaluate the checklist: Which items were useful? Which were ignored? What should be added or removed? This cycle of review ensures that the checklist remains relevant and effective. In the context of the Week 52 Review, the checklist becomes not just a preparation tool but also a record of what the class has learned about learning itself. It can be shared with parents or guardians to give them insight into the revision process, and it can serve as a starting point for discussions about study skills.

Passage 3: From Review to Action: Sustaining Improvement After the Annual Audit

A
The annual review is often seen as the end of a cycle, but in effective organisations, it is the beginning of the next. The Week 52 Review at Northbridge Adult Education Centre produced a set of decisions, but the real challenge lies in implementing them. Research on organisational change suggests that many improvement plans fail not because they are poorly designed but because they are not followed through. To avoid this, the centre has adopted a simple framework: assign responsibility, set deadlines, and monitor progress. This framework is deliberately lightweight, so that it does not become a burden in itself. The principal has emphasised that the framework should support staff, not add to their administrative load.

B
Assigning responsibility is the first step. For each action on the checklist, a specific person is named as the owner. For example, the simplification of the observation form was assigned to Mr. Patel, while the extension of online access was given to the IT manager, Mr. Li. This clarity ensures that everyone knows who is accountable and reduces the risk of tasks falling between the cracks. The principal also made it clear that owners are expected to report back at the October review meeting. In addition, each owner is encouraged to involve colleagues as needed, so that responsibility is shared rather than isolated. This collaborative approach helps to build ownership across the team.

C
Setting deadlines is equally important. Without deadlines, tasks can drift indefinitely. The centre set a deadline of the end of June for drafting the checklist, and specific deadlines for each action: the new observation form to be piloted by October, the online access to be extended by September, the storage room conversion to be completed by August, and the revised workshop format to be ready for the spring term. These deadlines are realistic but challenging, and they provide a clear timeline for everyone involved. The principal also suggested that interim milestones be set for larger tasks, so that progress can be tracked more frequently. For instance, the storage room conversion was divided into three stages: clearing the room, installing furniture, and setting up equipment.

D
Monitoring progress is the third element. The centre plans to use a simple tracking sheet where owners update the status of their actions monthly. The principal will review the tracking sheet before each staff meeting and follow up on any delays. This regular monitoring helps to identify problems early and allows for adjustments. For instance, if the tablet delivery is delayed again, the IT manager can inform the group and alternative arrangements can be made. The tracking sheet is kept online, so that all staff can view it and see how their colleagues are progressing. This transparency is intended to encourage cooperation rather than competition.

E
However, implementation is not only about systems; it is also about culture. The principal emphasised that the review should be seen as a supportive process, not a punitive one. Staff should feel comfortable reporting difficulties without fear of criticism. To foster this, the centre has introduced a “no-blame” policy for delays that are reported promptly. The focus is on finding solutions rather than assigning fault. This cultural shift is perhaps the most important factor in sustaining improvement. The principal has also started holding monthly coffee mornings where staff can raise concerns informally, which has helped to build trust.

F
Looking ahead, the centre plans to repeat the Week 52 Review next year, but with some refinements. The principal suggested that future reviews should include student representatives to gather their perspectives. She also proposed that the checklist be shared with students so they can see what the centre is working on. By involving all stakeholders, the review becomes a collaborative effort rather than a top-down audit. Ultimately, the goal is to create a culture of continuous improvement, where reflection leads to action and action leads to better outcomes for students. The centre also plans to publish an annual summary of its improvements on its website, so that the wider community can see the progress being made.

Listening Section 1: Social Dialogue

You will hear a conversation between a student, Maria, and a staff member at the university library, Tom.

Tom: Good morning, how can I help you?
Maria: Hi, I’m trying to find a quiet place to study for my exams. Is there a study room I can book?
Tom: Yes, we have several group study rooms, but they’re for groups of three or more. For individual study, you can use the silent zone on the second floor.
Maria: Oh, I see. Is the silent zone open all day?
Tom: It’s open from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. during exam weeks, but normally it closes at 8 p.m.
Maria: That’s good to know. Can I bring coffee in there?
Tom: I’m afraid not. Drinks are only allowed in the café area. But there are lockers near the entrance where you can leave your bag.
Maria: Okay. And do I need to book a seat in the silent zone?
Tom: No, it’s first-come, first-served. But it does get busy around lunchtime, so I’d recommend coming early.
Maria: Thanks. One more thing—are there any computers available?
Tom: Yes, there are ten computers in the silent zone, but you need your student card to log in.
Maria: Great, I have that. Thanks for your help!
Tom: You’re welcome. Good luck with your exams!

Listening Section 2: Social Monologue

You will hear a talk given by a student union representative about an upcoming event.

Hello everyone, I’m here to tell you about the annual Summer Fair, which will take place on Saturday, 15th June, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on the main campus field. This year’s fair is bigger than ever, with over 30 stalls selling food, crafts, and second-hand books. There will also be live music from local bands and a children’s play area.

We are still looking for volunteers to help set up and run the event. If you can spare two hours, please sign up at the student union office or online. Volunteers will receive a free lunch and a T-shirt.

One important change: this year, we are asking everyone to bring their own reusable cups and bags to reduce waste. There will be a water refill station near the entrance. Also, please note that parking on campus will be limited, so we encourage you to walk or use public transport.

The fair is open to everyone—students, staff, and the local community. We hope to see you there!

Listening Section 3: Academic Discussion

You will hear a discussion between two students, Anna and Ben, and their tutor, Dr. Green, about their research project on study habits.

Dr. Green: So, Anna and Ben, how is your project on study habits going?
Anna: We’ve collected data from 50 students, but we’re having trouble analysing it. We used a questionnaire with both multiple-choice and open-ended questions.
Ben: Yes, and the open-ended answers are quite varied. Some students wrote long paragraphs, others just a few words.
Dr. Green: That’s common. Have you considered coding the responses into categories?
Anna: We thought about that, but we’re not sure how to do it reliably.
Dr. Green: You could use thematic analysis. Start by reading through all the responses and noting recurring themes. Then define categories and assign each response to one or more categories. It helps to have two people code independently and then compare.
Ben: That sounds doable. Should we include the questionnaire in the appendix?
Dr. Green: Yes, definitely. And remember to report the response rate—how many students you approached versus how many completed it.
Anna: We approached 80 and got 50 back, so that’s about 62%.
Dr. Green: Good. Also, be careful about generalising from such a small sample. Acknowledge the limitations in your discussion.
Ben: We will. Thanks for the advice.

Listening Section 4: Academic Lecture

You will hear a lecture about the psychology of checklist design.

Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about why some checklists work and others fail, drawing on research in cognitive psychology and human factors. 

First, let’s consider the purpose of a checklist. A checklist is not simply a list of tasks; it is a tool to reduce errors, particularly in high-stakes environments like aviation and medicine. However, checklists are increasingly used in education, for example, to help students prepare for exams.

Research shows that checklists are most effective when they are concise. A long checklist can lead to “checklist fatigue,” where users stop paying attention. The ideal length is often cited as between five and nine items, though this can vary.

Second, checklists should focus on “killer items”—the steps that are most critical and most often missed. For example, in a writing exam, a killer item might be “check that you have answered all parts of the question.” 

Third, checklists should be used at the right time. In aviation, checklists are used before takeoff and before landing, not continuously. Similarly, in exams, a checklist is most useful at the end, to review your work, rather than at the beginning.

Finally, checklists need to be tested and refined. What works for one group may not work for another. By reviewing and updating checklists regularly, we can ensure they remain effective tools for improvement.

Thank you.

grammar.title: 整理仍会复现的错误：简短、可执行的考前检查单
grammar.explanation: 在英语写作和口语中，一些错误会反复出现，例如主谓一致、时态混用、冠词缺失、介词搭配错误等。制作一份简短的检查单，列出你最常犯的3-5个错误，并在每次练习后核对，可以有效减少这些错误。检查单应具体、可操作，例如“检查第三人称单数动词是否加-s”或“检查过去时是否一致”。
grammar.example: For instance, instead of writing “improve grammar,” a checklist item might say “check subject-verb agreement in the first paragraph.”

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
options: She go to school every day.
She goes to school every day.
She going to school every day.
She gone to school every day.
answers: She goes to school every day.
questions.explanation: 第三人称单数主语she后动词需加-s，go变为goes。
questions.evidence: She goes to school every day.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
options: I have seen that movie last week.
I saw that movie last week.
I see that movie last week.
I am seeing that movie last week.
answers: I saw that movie last week.
questions.explanation: last week是过去时间状语，需用一般过去时saw，不能用现在完成时。
questions.evidence: I saw that movie last week.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
options: He is interested in reading books.
He is interested on reading books.
He is interested at reading books.
He is interested for reading books.
answers: He is interested in reading books.
questions.explanation: 固定搭配be interested in，介词用in。
questions.evidence: He is interested in reading books.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
answers: The information is useful.
questions.explanation: information是不可数名词，谓语动词用单数is。
questions.evidence: The information is useful.
